nodes.title: Revisions
nodes.body:
1990 Jan 1. T. Duane Phillips; Mote Marine Laboratory
Note: Date Assigned based on when SLHs were written at Mote; Author based on Peter Rubec’s memory

nodes.title: TAXONOMY
nodes.body:
Common Name:  Scaled sardine
Scientific Name: Harengula jaguana

nodes.title: Classification
nodes.body:
Phylum: Chordata
	Class: Osteichthyes
	Order:  Clupeiformes
	Family: Clupeidae

Other Common Names:  bait, white bait, white minnow, minnow, sardine (664), pilchard, razorbelly (581).

nodes.title: VALUE & STATUS
nodes.body:
Commercial:  No major fishery exists in the United States (791).  Marketed fresh and canned in Cuba and Venezuela (791).  A small commercial fishery exists in south Florida for use as bait (1020).
Recreational:  An important bait fish in Florida (788 1020).

nodes.title: Indicator
nodes.body: Ecological Role:  Important prey for larger fishes such as Spanish mackerel and snappers (1020).  The fall run of Spanish mackerel coincides with peak seasonal abundance of clupeids, and scaled sardines were found to be particularly abundant in mackerel stomachs (382).

nodes.title: GEOGRAPHIC RANGE
nodes.body:
Overall:  Northeast Florida throughout the Gulf of Mexico, the Bahamas, the Caribbean to Brazil (327 788).
Within Study Area:  A common shore species along the Florida west coast.  Found throughout the Indian River Lagoon (887 997 1006).


Mobility and Migration:

nodes.title: Movement/Migration
nodes.body: A study in Florida Bay found that they move on and off the mud banks at dusk and dawn (852).  Diel migration is probably related to feeding on plankton (852).

nodes.title: BENTHIC HABITAT
nodes.body:
Habitat Type:  On the east coast of Florida, the scaled sardine is a dominant surf zone fish (Gilmore et al. 1981, Peters and Nelson 1987).  Additionally, Modde (479) found similar results at Horn Island, Mississippi.
Substrate:  Common over sand and mud bottoms (791 852).

nodes.title: Temperature
nodes.body:
Eggs/larvae:  Eggs were collected at temperatures between 20.8 and 30.7 C and larvae between 18.4 and 30.7 C (Houde 1977).  Larvae have the greatest survival at temperatures from 26-32 C (Saksena et al. 1972).
Juvenile/adults:  In Charlotte Harbor, taken in temperatures from 29o to 32 C (789).  Gaunter (255) collected them in Texas at temperatures ranging from 20.0 to 30.0 C but collected only nine specimens at temperatures less than 24 C.

nodes.title: Salinity
nodes.body:
Eggs/larvae: Eggs and larvae have been collected primarily at salinities > 35 % (Houde 1977).
Juvenile/adults:  In McKay Bay, Tampa Bay, large numbers are present in March and April when salinities are between 18 and 20 % (853).  Wang and Raney(789) collected them at salinities between 19.3 and 22.2 % in Charlotte Harbor.  Gaunter (255) reported a range of 4.8 to 36.9 % in Texas, but most were collected at salinities greater than 25 %.  More individuals occur in higher salinity areas than in low salinity areas in Florida Bay (851).

nodes.title: REPRODUCTION
nodes.body: Reproductive Mode:  Sexual reproduction with external fertilization.  Oviparous.

nodes.title: Mating/Spawning
nodes.body:
On the west coast of Florida, spawning occurs from January-September, but the highest concentration is from May-August (Houde 1977) and February and July (791).  On the east coast of Florida spawning occurs from February to August with a peak in April and May (1020).  Size at first maturity is 7.8 to 8.5 cm SL, and maturity is attained at one year of age (1020).  Peak spawning time is 2200 h (Houde 1977).
Fecundity: For individuals from 8.5 to 16.3 cm SL, fecundity ranged from 5,563 to 52,753.  Fecundity increases with size.  Relative fecundity is 548 ova per gram body weight and does not change significantly with size (1020).

nodes.title: Length Range
nodes.body:
Eggs:  Mean egg diameter is 1.66 mm.  There is a single, yellow oil globule in each egg  (Houde et al. 1973).
Larvae:  Mean daily growth ranged from 0.056 mm/day (21-23 C) to 1.035 mm/day (32 C) (Saksena et al. 1972).
Juveniles:  Transformation of larvae to juvenile occurred at 22-24 mm SL (Houde et al. 1973).
Adults:  Maximum size attained is 18 cm (788) and they are common to 12 cm (791).

nodes.title: FOOD HABITS
nodes.body: Known to feed on various planktonic crustaceans (581).  In Florida Bay, daily migration is probably related to feeding on plankton (852).
